metadata.summary: This EAACI position paper provides a comprehensive review and management recommendations for ocular allergy, covering seasonal and perennial allergic conjunctivitis, vernal and atopic keratoconjunctivitis, and contact blepharoconjunctivitis. It evaluates evidence for topical antihistamines, mast cell stabilizers, corticosteroids, calcineurin inhibitors, and allergen immunotherapy. The aim is to guide specialists in the treatment of these conditions.

conditions.description: Seasonal allergic conjunctivitis is an IgE-mediated hypersensitivity disorder of the conjunctiva triggered by seasonal airborne allergens, such as pollens.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Ocular itching, redness, tearing, and swelling that occur during specific seasons coinciding with allergen exposure.

conditions.name: Perennial Allergic Conjunctivitis
conditions.description: Perennial allergic conjunctivitis is an IgE-mediated hypersensitivity disorder of the conjunctiva triggered by year-round allergens, such as house dust mites, animal dander, or molds.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Chronic ocular itching, redness, tearing, and swelling with perennial, often fluctuating, symptoms.

conditions.name: Vernal Keratoconjunctivitis
conditions.description: Vernal keratoconjunctivitis is a persistent, chronic ocular allergic disorder with both IgE- and non-IgE-mediated mechanisms, often occurring in children and characterized by severe inflammation and potential corneal complications.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Severe ocular itching, photophobia, tearing, mucous discharge, giant papillae on the upper tarsal conjunctiva, and possible corneal involvement such as shield ulcers.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess conjunctival and corneal involvement (giant papillae, limbal infiltrates, corneal erosions).

diagnostic_workup.test: Allergy testing (skin prick or serum IgE)
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify contributing allergens, although VKC may not be solely IgE-driven.

conditions.name: Atopic Keratoconjunctivitis
conditions.description: Atopic keratoconjunctivitis is a severe, sight-threatening chronic allergic eye disease associated with atopic dermatitis, involving both IgE- and non-IgE-mediated pathways.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Eyelid eczema, intense itching, conjunctival inflammation, corneal damage, and potential visual impairment. Often associated with systemic atopy.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate eyelid, conjunctival, and corneal involvement.

diagnostic_workup.test: Allergy testing (skin prick or serum IgE)

conditions.name: Contact Blepharoconjunctivitis
conditions.description: Contact blepharoconjunctivitis is a non-IgE-mediated, delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction of the eyelids and conjunctiva caused by contact with allergens, such as cosmetics, topical medications, or environmental agents.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Eyelid eczema, itching, inflammation, and conjunctival involvement, often after exposure to a specific topical agent.

recommendations.statement: Vasoconstrictors alleviate only ocular hyperemia.
Vasoconstrictors should be used with caution and for only 5-7 days because of side effects and tachyphylaxis.
Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are effective for short-term use but do not target specific inflammatory mechanisms.
In adult patients with seasonal allergic conjunctivitis, leukotriene inhibitors are less effective than oral antihistamines.
Systemic antihistamines should be used when there are comorbidities requiring their use.
Some systemic antihistamines may cause ocular surface drying effects.

Topical corticosteroid eye drops should be used with caution under ophthalmologist monitoring and for as short a duration as possible due to the high risk of local and potentially blinding side effects.
For seasonal and perennial allergic conjunctivitis, topical corticosteroids are rarely needed.

Corticosteroid eye drops can be used as short pulsed therapy in acute exacerbations of ocular allergy, particularly in vernal and atopic keratoconjunctivitis or when the cornea is involved, under ophthalmologist supervision.
Intranasal corticosteroids are effective and well-tolerated for ocular symptoms associated with allergic rhinoconjunctivitis.
Intranasal corticosteroids should not be used if only ocular signs and symptoms are present.
Topical skin corticosteroid preparations should be used in the acute phase of eyelid eczema, with a preference for low-potency corticosteroids.
Cyclosporine A eye drops are not recommended for seasonal and perennial allergic conjunctivitis.
Cyclosporine A eye drops may be used as a steroid-sparing agent in steroid-dependent cases of vernal or atopic keratoconjunctivitis.
Tacrolimus off-label eye drops or ointment should be reserved for severe vernal and atopic keratoconjunctivitis cases refractory to cyclosporine A.
Allergen-specific immunotherapy may be considered when first-line treatments fail or to alter the natural course of ocular allergic disease.
Allergen-specific immunotherapy should only be considered when IgE-mediated hypersensitivity is confirmed.
Before recommending allergen-specific immunotherapy, control of allergic conjunctivitis symptoms and other systemic symptoms to assess suitability should be considered.
Allergen-specific immunotherapy is effective for the treatment of allergic conjunctivitis due to grass pollen.
Allergen-specific immunotherapy is effective for the treatment of allergic conjunctivitis due to house dust mite.
Sublingual immunotherapy effectively reduces total and individual ocular symptom scores in subjects with allergic conjunctivitis.
There are no studies on allergen-specific immunotherapy in vernal and atopic keratoconjunctivitis; in these forms, immunotherapy requires expert case-by-case assessment.

decision_rules: Start therapy with topical antihistamines, mast cell stabilizers, or dual-acting agents, as they are all effective in reducing signs and symptoms.

recommended_regimens.name: topical antihistamines, mast cell stabilizers, or dual-acting agents
recommended_regimens.summary: These agents are effective in reducing signs and symptoms of SAC. Dual-acting agents may provide quicker symptom relief and may be preferred. Specific agents include olopatadine, ketotifen, epinastine, and alcaftadine (only available in the US).
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Improvement in ocular symptom scores compared to placebo; no significant differences between individual agents in most studies; alcaftadine may offer superior itch relief.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Throughout the allergy season, as needed.

alternative_regimens.name: systemic antihistamines
alternative_regimens.summary: Oral antihistamines may be used when ocular symptoms are associated with other allergic comorbidities, such as rhinitis.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Concomitant allergic rhinitis or other systemic allergy symptoms.

alternative_regimens.name: intranasal corticosteroids
alternative_regimens.summary: Effective for ocular symptoms associated with allergic rhinoconjunctivitis, but should be reserved for patients with nasal symptoms.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Only if rhinitis is also present; not recommended for isolated ocular symptoms.

artifacts.title: Figure 2. Treatment algorithm for different forms and severities of ocular allergy
artifacts.description:
Algorithm for managing ocular allergy by subtype and severity:

1. Allergic Conjunctivitis (SAC/PAC): Start with avoidance, cold compresses, eyelid hygiene, and lubricants. If symptoms persist, use topical antihistamines, mast cell stabilizers, or dual-action agents (first-line). For moderate/severe cases or comorbid rhinitis, add systemic antihistamines. In acute exacerbations with corneal involvement, consider short-pulsed topical corticosteroids under ophthalmologist supervision. If steroid-dependent, switch to topical calcineurin inhibitors (cyclosporine, then tacrolimus). Consider allergen immunotherapy if specific sensitization is proven.

2. Vernal/AK Keratoconjunctivitis (VKC/AKC): Begin with avoidance of triggers, eyelid hygiene, and lubricants. For mild cases, start topical antihistamines or mast cell stabilizers. Moderate cases may require short-term topical corticosteroids; severe cases may need pulsed high-dose steroids. For steroid-dependent or severe corneal involvement, initiate topical cyclosporine (0.1% CE if available) or tacrolimus. Refractory cases may need systemic immunosuppression (cyclosporine, tacrolimus, mycophenolate). AIT may be considered on a case-by-case basis.

3. Contact Blepharoconjunctivitis (CBC): Management focuses on allergen avoidance, eyelid hygiene, emollients, and topical low-potency corticosteroids for eczema flares. Topical calcineurin inhibitor ointments can be used for lid eczema.
artifacts.summary: Stepwise therapeutic approach for ocular allergy, differentiating between mild/moderate SAC/PAC, severe VKC/AKC, and CBC, incorporating avoidance, pharmacotherapy, and immunotherapy as appropriate.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Guides clinicians through decision-making based on disease subtype and severity, ensuring appropriate escalation from topical agents to immunomodulators and specialist referral.

special_populations.considerations: Few reports on management in pregnant or lactating women. Allergen avoidance and environmental measures are first-line. Mast cell stabilizer eye drops can be used. Topical antihistamines or dual-acting drugs may be tried safely, though many are FDA category C. Short courses of topical corticosteroids are cautiously permitted if needed. Vasoconstrictors and decongestants are generally avoided. Systemic medications should be minimized. Second-generation oral antihistamines can be used (no teratogenic effects reported, low secretion in breast milk). Immunotherapy may be continued but not initiated during pregnancy.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Avoid vasoconstrictors/decongestants. Minimize systemic medications. Prefer second-generation oral antihistamines. Do not initiate immunotherapy; continuation only if already ongoing.

special_populations.considerations: Topical eye drops approved for adults are generally approved for children over 3 years old. Advise closing the punctum to reduce systemic absorption. First-generation antihistamines are not indicated due to sedative effects; second-generation antihistamines have a good long-term safety profile in pediatrics. Not licensed under 6 months of age.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Close punctum during drop instillation. Avoid first-generation antihistamines. Do not use in infants under 6 months.

special_populations.considerations: Ocular allergy may persist or appear de novo in the elderly. Age-related structural changes of the eyelid and ocular surface often mimic dry eye disease. Comorbidities and drug interactions limit treatment options. Systemic and local corticosteroids should be limited to short courses due to risks (diabetes, hypertension, osteoporosis, cataract, glaucoma). Topical and systemic decongestants and systemic antihistamines may cause dryness and should be avoided. Cumulative anticholinergic burden from antihistamines and other drugs must be considered.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Limit corticosteroid duration. Avoid decongestants and systemic antihistamines. Assess cumulative anticholinergic effects.
